text: As someone who’s been playing since before andesite, I got you. 1: Watch “Grian” on youtube. This is largely how I, and a lot of other people, learned how to build. He doesn't have individual house tutorials, but rather tutorials on how to improve your overall building skill. (I reccomend “how NOT to build” or “33 ways to improve your house” to start with)2: Avoid flat surfaces, depth is detail. Looking at a house with a ledge or a frame around it is much more appealing than a flat wall3: pallet, switch up the blocks you use. You can even use darker blocks at the bottom and lighter ones at the top for a nice “gradient” effect. If you google “minecraft block pallets” theres one or 2 websites with tons of suggestions. I personally like to use a lot of stone, andesite, spruce wood (especially stripped logs) and moss 4: Shaping. This could very well be the most important one yet. If you’re going to make a big house, don’t make a giant square. Rectangles look good all the time, but big square boxes never look good. T-shapes or even just going wild with an outline can massively improve the design.

text: Add dimension! I know it sounds weird and wasteful but it will make a big difference- take your logs on the side, and pull them towards the front of the house by one block. text: Layers on layers. Look at buildings in real life and other people builds, the main thing you will notice is that things aren’t just flat. Bring your corner pillars out diagonally one block and make a support truss going across connecting them(you can use stairs to make diagonal lines from the cross to the roof to put more detail), extend the roof to cover the extra space(real houses do this for drainage), add some flower boxes, windows with trapdoors around them for depth(spruce on either side looks like storm shudders), try different roof designs using a mix of slabs and stairs to end up with a shorter less peaked roof, throw a chimney up there somewhere with a campfire to make it look like you have a fire going inside. Minecraft has a ton of blocks to choose from, throw a bunch down and see how you like the pallet. Stone types make a strong looking roof but can look out of place if the house looks like it would collapse under the weight. Different wood types fit different places, darker woods look weathered like they are an exterior thing(but can absolutely work inside) while lighter woods like birch make a brighter more “welcoming” interior. The creativity goes as far as you will take it.

text: Make the roof and walls and floors out of different materials. They could all still be wood, but vary the type at least. Otherwise you end up with this 'one solid colour' look. You did good adding some corner logs, but what about cross beams too? Generally houses aren't constructed with just upright beams, they have ones resting across to add support too. This will help in separating the roof from the walls too. Rooves tend to overhang walls a little, so the roof could do with being one space further out on ALL sides. Again, this will break up the shape a bit. Having roof, wall or floor all being one colour is boring, but more importantly it shows far too much of the same repeating texture to be beautiful to our eyes. It's a solid flat shape, and solid flat shapes are usually bad! Try adding windows, window borders and decoration (trapdoors, flowerpots etc), foundations of stone that go up one block from the floor, stairs and slabs can be used to add even more depth. Nature! You can easily break up solid shape and add more detail by planting a few bushes against the wall. Even better - some leafy growths that climb up the wall and over the roof can tie the whole thing together. Square houses are BAD. Add an extension, figure out how the roof can look good while attached there (look at some real world examples!) Practice! My biggest piece of advice here is to build a small 5x7 house with a roof and add a little extension. Then build another next to it with different materials and designs. Eventually you'll start to figure out colour pallets you like and will develop your own unique style to your builds.

text: I prefer three styles: depth: when I build with the same materials, I build on 2, 3 levels, a lot with steps and walls. Here the Deepslate variants and stone are very suitable. textures: If a wall should be flat or there is not enough space for thick walls, you can also mix several color matching blocks. In your case straped logs are suitable, perhaps also different colored wood. Here I always try to build "patches", but many others mix the blocks chaotically. I don't think it makes a difference - I just try to tell a story when I build. :D Try there in Creative which colors of blocks you just have available fit. gradients: With very high structures there is a great effect to let the textures get lighter towards the top. So you can go from mud to jungle wood and calcite to snow and quartz. Which works wonders for simple houses: Make the first floor out of a stone and put wood on top. Also, details are worth a lot, a flower box here, a hanging lantern there... When you work with textures or gradients, don't think too much about logic. Acacia logs in particular are great for "mechanical" buildings and the straped variant looking very well with copper. You can also get inspiration from youtubers, Grian has a lot of "building tutorials" - I'm sure there are some more.

text: Add depth to your walls. Push things in or out a block to add depth. For example you can move those logs outwards. Never have a completely flat wall with one block type. Try to have 2 or 3 blocks of depth with features at multiple levels. Use a multitude of blocks. Blocks that have colour that complement each other work together. The most common palette is two colours that contrast or complement eachother and a variety of textures in both colours. For example wood and stone work together well well and using planks, logs, stripped wood for the brown colours and then stone, cobblestone, stone bricks and adesite for the grey colours. Use blocks that aren't cubes. Things like buttons, stairs, fences, wallls, ladders all add detail to your build. Make your layout interesting. For a house specifically experiment with different shaped room, amount of stories, the height of each stories, connections between rooms. Don't always stick to a grid for rooms. Add exterior features. If you have a flat wall with nothing maybe add a window that can have a planter box or a balcony area. Add a chimney or lightning rood to the roof. Anything you might expect to be attached to the outside of a building. Have a progression upwards. Usually this is done by adding a strip at the bottom of the walls. But having your building visually slightly change as it goes upwards is very good. Don't follow any of this strictly. But take what you can and use it. Happy building.

text: The main thing here is that it needs more depth. Everything looks flat. I recreated your build so I can show you what I mean and how to fix it: Faithful recreation First, bring those log corners out a block. Like so This adds more depth/dimension to it instead of a boring flat wall. Next, make the roof a different type of block than the normal wall, to break up the shape a bit and make it more interesting. I used brick for example. Next, similar to the log posts, bring the roof out. To do that, you'll need to do a diagonal effect. You can do that by placing stairs underneath each other at the right angle, demonstrated here: Diagonal stairs, with 2 different types of blocks to make it easier to see Now to put it into practice. First lengthen it on the sides Then lengthen it up front Then lengthen it again up front to cover up those logs posts a bit. Now this is just personal preference, but I like to remove the roofing material from the front wall. If you're feeling fancy, instead of replacing it with your basic wall material you can throw in another material here.
